summaries.example: Imagine a box of puzzle pieces. “Every piece in the box is blue” is like saying something is necessary: it is true in every case we are considering. “Some piece could be red” is like saying it is possible: it is true in at least one case. Modal logic helps us reason carefully about words such as “must,” “could,” “always,” and “ought.”
summaries.summary: Modal logic studies careful reasoning about ideas such as necessity and possibility. It also includes logics about what is required or allowed, what was or will be the case, what someone believes or knows, and what would happen under an imagined condition. Logicians use symbols, rules, and models of possible situations to check arguments. A possible-world model assigns statements different truth values in different situations. A statement is necessary when it is true in every relevant situation, and possible when it is true in at least one. The entry explains that there is not just one modal logic. Different meanings of words such as “must,” “ought,” and “always” call for different systems. These ideas also help describe computer programs, games, and the steps a system may take.
key_ideas: “Necessary” means true in every relevant situation; “possible” means true in at least one relevant situation.
Modal logic has related branches for duties, time, belief, knowledge, and conditionals.
Different rules fit different meanings. What is necessary is not the same as what is required or what happened in the past.
Possible-world models help logicians test arguments instead of relying only on ordinary-language guesses.
Modal logic is used in philosophy and in computer science, including reasoning about programs and their possible steps.
summaries.why_it_matters: People often use words like “must,” “can,” “ought,” and “always” quickly, even though they can mean different things. Modal logic makes those differences visible. It can help us examine arguments, describe rules and time, and represent choices or pathways in computer systems. Learning its basic ideas encourages us to ask: Which situations are relevant, and what exactly does the modal word apply to?

important_terms.definition: A word or symbol that changes how a statement is understood, such as “must,” “may,” “always,” or “ought.”
The study of reasoning about what must be true and what could be true. It also includes related kinds of logic about time, duties, belief, and knowledge.
A way to represent a situation we are considering. A possible world need not be a real planet; it can be a different way things might be.
A statement that says something must be true.
A statement that says something might be true.
A link that tells us which situations count as relevant when we decide whether a modal statement is true.

questions_to_think_about: Is something that is required always something that actually happens?
What different situations should count when we say that something is “possible”?
Why might “If this happens, then that must happen” have more than one meaning?
Can a computer use rules about possible steps to check whether a program works?

summaries.example: Suppose a program is at state s and can make two moves, leading to states t and u. The claim “after this program step, the computer will be safe” is true at s only if safety holds at both t and u. The claim “the computer can become safe after this step” is true if safety holds at at least one of them. This illustrates the role of an accessibility relation: it identifies which successor states matter. In a temporal system, the relation may mean “later than”; in a game system, it may mean “a move available to player i.”
summaries.summary: Modal logic is formally the study of deduction involving necessity and possibility, represented by operators often written as □ and ◇. In a broader sense it is a family of systems for obligation and permission, past and future, belief and knowledge, counterfactuals, provability, and related notions. K provides a weak base; systems such as M, S4, and S5 add principles governing truth, iteration, and the structure of modal alternatives. The acceptability of these principles depends on the intended interpretation, since ordinary language uses modal expressions in several ways and can hide differences in scope. Possible-world semantics gives a precise account: a frame contains worlds and an accessibility relation, while a valuation assigns truth values at worlds. Conditions on the relation correspond to axioms, and soundness and completeness connect formal proofs with semantic validity. The entry also discusses two-dimensional semantics for indexicals and actuality, provability logic, quantified modal logic, bisimulation, frame correspondence, and modal analyses of games and computation.
key_ideas: The narrow subject of modal logic is necessity and possibility, but the wider family includes deontic, temporal, doxastic, epistemic, conditional, and provability logics.
The basic system K supplies a foundation, while additional axioms such as M, 4, B, and 5 impose stronger patterns on modal operators.
The choice of axiom depends on interpretation. For example, “necessarily” may require reflexivity, while “always in the future” need not imply that the statement is true now.

Possible-world semantics replaces ordinary truth tables with worlds, valuations, and an accessibility relation. Frame conditions such as reflexivity, transitivity, seriality, or symmetry can correspond to axioms.
Natural-language scope matters: “If A, then necessarily B” can differ from “It is necessary that if A, then B.”
Modal methods extend into computer science, where they describe program transitions, information, strategies, and equivalence of processes.
summaries.why_it_matters: Modal reasoning appears whenever an argument concerns what could happen, what must happen, what should happen, what has happened, or what an agent knows. Formal systems expose ambiguities that ordinary grammar can conceal and provide ways to compare competing interpretations. Their semantic models also have practical significance: accessibility relations can represent program transitions, game moves, times, or information states. The subject therefore links philosophical analysis with mathematical logic and computer science while preserving an important caution: no single modal system automatically fits every use of modal language.

important_terms.definition: An expression that qualifies a judgment by indicating necessity, possibility, obligation, permission, time, belief, or knowledge.
A formal system of axioms and inference rules intended to capture valid reasoning for a particular interpretation of modal expressions.
A set of situations used to evaluate modal claims. A sentence is necessary, in the simplest semantics, when it is true at every relevant world.
A structure consisting of worlds and a relation specifying which worlds are relevant or reachable from each world.
The relation connecting a world to the worlds relevant for evaluating its modal claims. Its properties can correspond to modal axioms.
A formal property stating that every theorem produced by a system is valid under its semantics.
A formal property stating that every argument valid under a semantics can be proved in the system.
A logic of obligation, permission, and prohibition. Its rules need not say that every obligation is actually fulfilled.

questions_to_think_about: Why should the axiom that necessary truths are true be accepted for necessity but rejected for obligation or future tense?
What changes when an accessibility relation is transitive, reflexive, or serial?
How does the scope of “necessarily” change the difference between □(A→B) and A→□B?
Should a quantified modal logic use one fixed domain of objects or domains that vary from world to world?
What information about a program or game is preserved by a bisimulation, and what information may be ignored?

summaries.example: Think about a school rule: “Students must return library books.” This does not mean every student actually returns a book. It says the action is required. In modal logic, that difference matters. A necessity claim says something is true in every relevant possibility. An obligation claim says something is required, even if people fail to do it. A temporal claim is different again: “Students will always have access to the library” concerns future times. The same sentence pattern cannot safely be given the same rule in all three cases.
summaries.summary: Modal logic examines reasoning about necessity and possibility, then extends the same general approach to obligation, permission, time, belief, knowledge, conditionals, provability, and more. The entry presents a basic system called K and explains how additional axioms produce systems with different strengths. These systems cannot be judged apart from interpretation: an axiom suitable for necessity may be wrong for obligation or tense. Possible-world semantics makes the differences precise by assigning truth values to statements at worlds connected by an accessibility relation. The relation can represent relevant alternatives, later times, morally acceptable outcomes, or available computer moves. Its properties—such as reflexivity, transitivity, and seriality—correspond to important axioms. The entry also explains why soundness and completeness matter, how modal logic supports analysis of games and programs, and why adding quantifiers creates difficult choices about objects that exist in different worlds.
key_ideas: Modal logic studies more than one meaning of “must” or “could,” so different modal systems may be appropriate for different purposes.
K is a basic system. Adding axioms creates stronger systems, but stronger is not automatically better; the axioms must match the intended interpretation.
Possible worlds are tools for evaluating claims. They can represent alternatives, future moments, morally acceptable outcomes, or states of a computer process.
Properties of the accessibility relation explain why particular axioms work. Reflexivity is linked with M, transitivity with 4, and seriality with D.
Modal operators can be combined with operators for time, knowledge, belief, agency, and preference, especially when analyzing games and information.
Quantified modal logic raises a further question: does the range of objects stay fixed across worlds, or can different worlds contain different objects?
summaries.why_it_matters: Modal words shape everyday reasoning, from promises and rules to predictions and explanations. They are also easy to misunderstand because the same word can be used with different scopes or standards of relevance. Modal logic gives us a disciplined way to compare those meanings. Beyond philosophy, its models can represent time, choices, information, and computer processes, making it useful for asking whether a system behaves correctly in every allowed path or in at least one possible path.

important_terms.definition: A way of changing a statement to show that it is necessary, possible, required, permitted, forbidden, past, future, believed, or known.
A group of formal logics that studies necessity and possibility and also related ideas such as duties, time, belief, and knowledge.
A formal picture containing situations or “worlds” and information about which worlds are relevant from each one.
A relation that selects the worlds, times, or states that count as reachable or relevant from a given one.
A logic about duties, permissions, and prohibitions. It does not assume that what ought to happen actually happens.
A logic about past and future. Operators can say that something always was, was at some point, will always be, or will occur at some point.
A system is sound when everything it proves is valid according to its semantics.
A system is complete when every argument valid according to its semantics can be proved in that system.

questions_to_think_about: Why is “what ought to happen” not guaranteed to be “what happens”?
When might two people use the word “possible” while considering different sets of relevant situations?
How could confusing □(A→B) with A→□B change the meaning of an argument?
Would a model of a computer program need to include every imaginable state, or only states reachable by its instructions?
What might be gained, and what might be lost, by allowing the objects in a domain to vary from world to world?
